items.title: What’s Coming in WordPress 7.2? (Features and Screenshots)
items.desc: WordPress 7.2 beta is out. See what's coming: Notes in the margin, the new Ipsum default theme, form styling without CSS, a faster admin, and /random/ links. The post What’s Coming in WordPress 7.2? (Features and Screenshots) first appeared on WPBeginner .
items.full: WordPress 7.2 beta is now available for testing. We have been testing it on a demo coffee shop blog since Beta 1, and this one is shaping up to be a practical update for everyday site owners. The WordPress core team plans to release the final version on December 8, 2026, which makes it the last major WordPress release of the year. There’s a lot to cover, from Notes that sit in the margin of your post to form styling without code and a faster admin area. Read on to see what’s coming in WordPress 7.2 and what it means for your website. TL;DR: What’s coming in WordPress 7.2 Note: This beta release is for testing and development only. So, please do not install, run, or test this version of WordPress on your live website. Instead, we recommend using a staging site or a local site. You can test WordPress 7.2 Beta by installing and activating the WordPress Beta Tester plugin. Notes have improved with every release since they arrived in WordPress 6.9 . WordPress 7.1 added @mentions and notes on selected text. In 7.2, the focus is on making Notes easier to see and use while you write. The biggest change is where Notes live. Instead of sitting inside a sidebar, notes now float in the margin of the editor canvas, right next to the block they belong to. This works much like comments in Google Docs. In our testing, we left notes on a draft as two different team members. WordPress highlighted each commented block in its author’s color, which made it easy to see who asked for what at a glance. Now that Notes no longer take up the sidebar, you can keep them open at the same time as the block settings panel. Previously, opening one closed the other, which was annoying when you wanted to fix a block while reading the feedback about it. Other Notes improvements include: For teams, agencies, and multi-author blogs, these small changes add up. Reviewing a draft inside WordPress is starting to feel like a natural part of your editorial workflow instead of a workaround. WordPress 7.2 will ship with a new default theme called Ipsum. Ipsum is an intentionally minimal block theme for bloggers. It takes its name from “lorem ipsum,” the placeholder text designers use until real content arrives. The theme follows the same idea. It gives you a clean starting point that you can turn into your own design. Ipsum includes several style variations that change the colors and typography of the whole site, including images. It also comes with patterns for headers, post lists, footers, and callouts. Ipsum also breaks a 16-year tradition. Since Twenty Ten, WordPress has named every default theme after its year, like Twenty Twenty-Five, and future default themes will get their own names instead. In our testing, Ipsum came with 8 color variations and 6 typography sets. You can find them in Appearance » Editor » Styles » Browse styles. One click on a variation like ‘Golden Hour’ restyles the whole site, including the images. Ipsum also works well with agentic AI tools like WPVibe , which connects your site to the AI assistant you already use, like Claude or ChatGPT. items.full: More than 50 educational institutions have joined WordPress Credits , giving students worldwide a way to earn academic recognition for contributing to WordPress. The program had two participating institutions in September 2025 and four the following month. By June 2026, that number had reached 27, before passing 50 this October. The program launched with the University of Pisa and was announced at WordCamp Europe 2025. Since then, it has expanded through partnerships that connect students with experienced contributors and practical projects. The WordPress Credits dashboard recorded participating institutions across 17 countries as of October 19, including Bangladesh, Costa Rica, Spain, Bolivia, and Indonesia. Each institution can adapt the program to its academic requirements, allowing students to contribute as part of their studies. Students work with mentors on projects that reflect their interests and areas of study. They might translate WordPress, improve documentation, create learning materials, or contribute to development and testing. Alongside that work, they practice collaborating with others and responding to feedback, then present their contributions at the end of the program. By October 19, the dashboard recorded 364 graduates and student contributions across 18 WordPress teams. That work supports the software and resources people use throughout the WordPress community. Local contributors have helped establish these partnerships by introducing WordPress Credits to nearby schools and adapting it to local languages and educational settings. Mentors guide students through their first contributions, while sponsors provide support and resources. Educators help make that participation part of students’ academic work. Thank you to the students, educators, mentors, and supporters whose involvement has brought the program to more than 50 institutions. Institutions can include WordPress Credits in an existing course, offer it as an internship, or incorporate it into a final project. The program is available at no cost to partner institutions, with flexible formats to suit their students and curriculum. To get started, read how to launch a WordPress Credits program and register your institution’s interest through the program page .

items.title: CSS-Tricks, Version 20
items.desc: Things look a little different around here? I hope so because we just pushed a site redesign! Here's everything new with the 20th(!!) version of CSS-Tricks. CSS-Tricks, Version 20 originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago . That’s ancient in web (and dog) years. It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024 , but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage. Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the new v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump. Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why. Excavating Ghosts First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust. For example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML <details> . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB). I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme. There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out. Modern Dev Tooling Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits: For years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here. Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. items.title: Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer
items.desc: Tencent chief AI scientist Vinces Yao Shunyu warns that AI will soon be able to develop bioweapons and argues for a middle ground between open and closed models. While safety filters on open-source systems can be easily stripped through abliteration, closed models like Anthropic's Claude often block too aggressively. For its upcoming open-weight model Hy4, Tencent is filtering dangerous hacking knowledge directly from the training data. The article Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Tencent's AI chief says AI bioweapons are coming, but closing off models isn't the answer Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 9, 2026 GPT-Image-2 prompted by THE DECODER Tencent's chief AI scientist warns that AI will soon be capable of developing bioweapons, and neither fully open nor fully closed models can solve this problem on their own. In the debate over open versus closed AI models, Vinces Yao Shunyu , formerly at OpenAI, is arguing for a middle ground, according to the South China Morning Post . A mix of open-source and closed-source lets everyone use the technology for defense as well. In biology, though, offensive and defensive capabilities are harder to separate than in cybersecurity. Since the gap between Chinese and US models isn't large, Yao urges the entire industry to proceed carefully. Yao says Anthropic and other US companies have made strong arguments for closed models, but he also sees clear advantages in open ones. He points to a hacking incident at Hugging Face as an example: when closed US models like Anthropic's Claude refused to analyze attack commands because of their safety filters, the platform used the open Chinese model GLM-5.2 to parse the logs instead. The Hugging Face report backs up Yao's example but also shows its limits. GLM-5.2 was only used during the forensic analysis. The actual attack was stopped when the security team patched the exploited vulnerability, rebuilt affected servers, and rotated credentials. Hugging Face also stressed that the incident isn't an argument against safety filters on hosted models. In July, Anthropic was the only major AI lab that didn't sign an Nvidia-backed letter warning against premature restrictions on open models. CEO Dario Amodei pushes back specifically against the claim that open models benefit defenders more than attackers. He argues they're potentially riskier because safety mechanisms are hard to enforce and published model weights can't be taken back. Anthropic doesn't call for an outright ban on open models, though. A technique called Abliteration shows how fragile safety filters are on open models. Anyone with access to a model's weights can use it to surgically remove trained refusal behaviors. Thousands of these modified variants sit on Hugging Face, and the US startup Abliteration.ai sells access to an unfiltered version of GLM-5.3. Current research shows that existing countermeasures make these modifications harder but don't prevent them. A more robust approach is to keep dangerous knowledge out of the model during training in the first place. China recognizes the problem too. The standards body TC260 warns that safety mechanisms in open models can be removed or bypassed and is working on its own security standard for open-source AI. A draft export control framework covers particularly large models but exempts open models that have already been released. Neither China nor the US has set a binding threshold above which open models can't be published. items.title: Google ships four TPU variants in one year as it ramps up competition with Nvidia
items.desc: Google is expanding its TPU 8 family with two specialized variants: the TPU 8tx keeps sensitive data encrypted even during processing, while the TPU 8i Max doubles compute power and memory by placing two chips on a single package. With nearly 100 external customers now on board, Google is increasingly positioning its in-house chips as an alternative to Nvidia's GPUs. The article Google ships four TPU variants in one year as it ramps up competition with Nvidia appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: With two new TPU variants, Google is targeting confidential AI workloads and memory-hungry applications. The expansion cements Google's strategic shift toward positioning its in-house AI chips as a broad platform for external customers. Google has added two new systems to its eighth-generation AI accelerator lineup: the TPU 8tx for confidential computing and the TPU 8i Max for memory-intensive workloads. With these additions, Google says it has shipped four TPU systems within a single year for the first time. Both new variants are built on existing silicon. Google isn't introducing a new chip generation here, but new system configurations: different packaging, different networking, and different memory setups around the same processor. The company frames this modular approach as a deliberate design choice that lets it deliver new hardware variants in months rather than years. Ad The TPU 8tx targets enterprises and government agencies working with confidential data. Normally, data is encrypted during storage and transmission but has to be decrypted in memory once a processor works with it. Ad The TPU 8tx is designed to close that gap. According to Google, data and model weights stay protected and isolated even during active use. Nvidia already offers a comparable feature for GPUs through its confidential computing architecture. The system uses the same low-latency Boardfly network Google developed for real-time inference and is supposed to deliver up to twice the latency reduction compared to the TPU 8t. Google says enterprises can use a single system to fine-tune models, distill large models into smaller ones, and train AI agents with reinforcement learning, all without moving sensitive data between different clusters. Ad The TPU 8i Max tackles a different problem: the memory bottleneck. When AI agents work simultaneously across large codebases or hours of video, memory bandwidth becomes the chokepoint. Google addressed this by placing two TPU 8i chips on a single package. The result is double the compute power, double the memory, and double the memory bandwidth in the same rack format, which means significantly more performance per square meter of data center space. Ad Beyond hardware, Google is working to make TPUs easier to use. The company has released TorchTPU as open source , so PyTorch code should run on TPUs with minimal changes. Popular inference frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are also supported. Ad The expansion is a direct response to Google's strategic shift from treating TPUs as a purely internal tool to marketing them as a competitive platform for outside customers. The company now counts nearly 100 external TPU customers. A broader market trend is driving this push. As AI applications spread, the focus is shifting from expensive training runs to inference, meaning the day-to-day operation of models. Specialized chips like TPUs can play to their strengths in exactly this area. That's also why Amazon, Microsoft, and OpenAI are all developing their own accelerators. items.title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
items.desc: Consciousness researchers Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi argue in a Nature commentary that today's AI systems aren't conscious and won't become so on silicon hardware. They consider the assumption that consciousness depends on computation alone "fatally flawed" and warn against granting rights to AI systems. The article The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate Manuel Uth Nov 8, 2026 Three leading consciousness researchers argue today's AI isn't conscious and probably can't be on silicon hardware. They reject the idea that running the right computations is enough for consciousness, challenging a central assumption in the debate. Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Giulio Tononi have spent decades researching consciousness from the perspectives of experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology, and philosophy of mind. Their commentary responds to voices like biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton , who consider AI systems possibly already conscious. In their commentary for Nature , the authors also point to a study Anthropic published this year. The company reported internal processing patterns in Claude that resemble properties of consciously accessible information processing. Anthropic doesn't see this as evidence of subjective experience. To understand the scope of the commentary, it helps to look at the report "Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence" by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long, and 17 other experts, including AI researcher Yoshua Bengio. The team drew on leading neuroscientific theories about how consciousness arises in the human brain and derived a kind of checklist with 14 indicators. The more of these an AI system meets, the stronger the case that it could be conscious. The researchers then evaluated several current systems, including large language models like GPT-4. The report concludes that none of the systems examined is a strong candidate for consciousness. On that point, it aligns with Seth, Block, and Tononi. For language models, Butlin and colleagues found only weak signs that the models meet the indicators of one of the most prominent consciousness theories at all. At the same time, the report sees no obvious technical barriers to building future AI systems that meet more indicators . Whether such systems would actually be conscious remains open. The authors specifically softened an earlier, stronger formulation on this point. There's also a foundational assumption. The team assumed that consciousness depends solely on the type of information processing, not on whether it happens in nerve cells or computer chips. Experts call this computational functionalism. The authors adopted this assumption explicitly "for pragmatic reasons" because it's what makes it possible to examine AI systems for consciousness in the first place. The report itself acknowledged that its indicators would no longer be reliable if consciousness is tied to properties of living organisms. It cited Anil Seth, among others, as a proponent of that opposing view. That's where the Nature commentary picks up. The authors argue that consciousness is what disappears during dreamless sleep or general anesthesia and returns when you wake up or dream. Drawing on philosopher Thomas Nagel, they describe it this way: "Conscious experiences feel like something." Intelligence, by contrast, means carrying out functions. items.title: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts
items.desc: Turing Award winner Richard Sutton reaffirms that raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence and that fundamentally new learning methods are needed. Ex-OpenAI researcher Tworek agrees, saying blind transformer scaling "has reward hacked brains of a whole generation of scientists." A growing wave of startups is already betting on exactly this gap. The article The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM scaling enthusiasts appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The inventor of the bitter lesson has a bitter lesson for LLM enthusiasts. Other researchers agree. In a recent post, Turing Award winner Richard Sutton says raw compute alone isn't enough for intelligence. AI science needs clever new methods and is "far from finished." His post sparked wide discussion in the AI community on X , a sign that Sutton struck a nerve. In his famous 2019 essay "The Bitter Lesson," Sutton argued that general methods scaling with compute beat sophisticated human-engineered approaches eventually. What matters are ideas that grow with compute rather than rely on human assumptions. Ad Sutton's position isn't new. In earlier statements , he criticized the limits of simply scaling large language models. He called synthetic data a "big mistake" because the real world is infinitely complex and any simulation of it is only "microscopic." Human expertise as a bottleneck prevents true scaling. Ad Instead, he called for agents with world models that continuously learn from their own experience. The world is massively more complex than what internet text can capture, and today's language models don't keep learning after training, Sutton argues. What's needed is continuous learning without destroying old knowledge. AI researcher Jerry Tworek, who like many others left OpenAI, one of the major AI companies, to explore new AI approaches, puts Sutton's latest statement in context. The bitter lesson still holds, but the more compute goes into model training, the more the algorithm matters, Tworek writes. Ad Some algorithms scale, others hit dead ends, and many dimensions of scaling remain completely unexplored. The temporary success of transformer scaling, combined with a misreading of the bitter lesson, "has reward-hacked the brains of a whole generation of scientists." AI researcher Jayden Teoh adds another angle. He says he has repeatedly seen the bitter lesson hold back academic research, with promising ideas dismissed for straying too far from its spirit. Teoh argues that this is not Sutton’s fault but a misreading of his original message. Ad Teoh also argues that ideas that seemed, in hindsight, not to follow the bitter lesson were often replaced by cleaner, more general approaches. That did not make those ideas wrong, he says; they were often what enabled progress at the time. He wants the research community to stop dismissing such work as soon as it appears. “An idea doesn’t necessarily have to survive scaling forever to be an important contribution to AI progress,” Teoh writes. Ad The tension between Sutton's call for new learning methods and Tworek's criticism of blind transformer scaling shows up in a growing wave of startups. In the latest Frontier Radar #5 , we tracked 45 new AI labs betting on exactly these gaps. Tworek himself runs Core Automation , one of those labs, searching for learning algorithms beyond pretraining and reinforcement learning. What unites these founders, including Sutton with Oak Lab , is that they believe in much more capable AI but doubt today's recipe alone will get there. items.title: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small AI model built for the repetitive work agents actually do
items.desc: Meta is introducing Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model, optimized for repetitive agent tasks such as tool calls, routing, and data extraction. According to Meta, it delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna. But it falls short when it comes to actual programming tasks. The article Meta launches Muse Ember, a small AI model built for the repetitive work agents actually do appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Meta has introduced Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model to date. It's designed for the routine tasks AI agents handle all day: calling tools, handling small coding tasks, routing requests, extracting data, and processing long documents. Meta says Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar at every reasoning level than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna. It costs about $0.14 per task in the Artificial Analysis test , while the larger Muse Spark 1.3 costs $2.39 for a nearly identical score of 36 versus 37. Muse Ember leads in most of Meta's own tests, but Haiku outperforms it on real coding tasks in FrontierCode 2.0-AA, scoring 34.9 percent to Muse Ember's 27.2 percent. The model handles text, images, audio, and video and can process up to one million tokens at once. It's available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.
